newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi Arabia opens to private investment funds.
newsitem.headline: Saudi Arabia opens to private investment funds.

text.p: A $650 million link between U.S. oil major Chevron Corp and Saudi businessmen to build and operate a petrochemical plant in Saudi Arabia is an important part of Riyadh's drive to stimulate private investment in its industrial sector, economists in Riyadh said on Wednesday.

Chevron Corp's Chevron Chemical Co and the Saudi Industrial Venture Capital Group announced in California on Tuesday the formation of a 50-50 joint venture to build and operate the greenfield plant at the eastern coastal city of Jubail.
The joint company is lining up the biggest single private investment in Saudi Arabia's expanding petrochemical sector.
Petrochemicals have been singled out by the government as the cornerstone of industrial development and a way for Riyadh to cut its dependency on huge, but volatile, oil earnings.
"This is a step in the direction that government policy has been set," said Anzar Ahmed, vice-president of the Riyadh-based Consulting Centre for Finance and Investment.

The industry is expected to grow at an annual rate of 8.3 percent in the years 1995-2000 covered by the five-year plan -- outpacing 3.8 percent growth in oil and gas -- to contribute $1.2 billion to GDP by 2000, Ministry of Planning forecasts show.
Saudi Arabia is the Middle East's biggest petrochemicals producer.

Foreign investors have had a presence in the country's petrochemical business since the 1980s but this has been in partnership with the majority state-owned and dominant local industrial concern Saudi Basic Industries Corp (SABIC).
"The deal is proof that the Saudi petrochemical sector is wide open for private investors...the government policy is clear," one Riyadh economist, who declined to be named, said.

The Chevron-Saudi venture will followed this year and next by other petrochemical investments by Saudi and foreign firms, including the local Alujain Corp which is expected next month to make an investment decision on its plans to build a 800,000 tonnes a year plant to produce the gasoline oxygenate MTBE.
Other privately-backed projects in the pipeline include plants to produce a range of plastics, fibres and resins.
The Chevron-Saudi plant, due on stream in 1999-2000 will manufacture 480,000 tonnes a year of benzene from a natural gasoline feedstock supplied by state oil company Saudi Aramco.

Potential private petrochemical investors had been unsure of their plans after the Saudi government denied a licence to a proposed petrochemical joint venture between Mobil Corp and a group of Saudi private investors in 1993.
The government made its position clear a year later when it said it would welcome private investment.
Foreign firms are not permitted equity or production sharing rights in the kingdom's prolific oil and gas fields but are present in oil refining, marketing and petrochemicals.
